content: Cytochrome c1, also referred to as CYC1, is a heme-containing mitochondrial protein encoded by the CYC1 gene in humans. It is also known by other names, including UQCR4, MC3DN6, Complex III subunit 4, Cytochrome b-c1 complex subunit 4, and Ubiquinol-cytochrome-c reductase complex cytochrome c1 subunit. This protein functions as a respiratory subunit of Ubiquinol Cytochrome c Reductase, also known as complex III, which is a critical component of the electron transport chain located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Mutations in the CYC1 gene can result in mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear, type 6. The CYC1 gene is located on the long (q) arm of chromosome 8 at position 24.3 and consists of 8 exons. The protein encoded by this gene has a molecular weight of 13.5 kDa and is composed of 130 amino acids. CYC1 is a member of the cytochrome c family and is classified as a phosphoprotein. It is a subunit of Ubiquinol Cytochrome c Reductase and is capable of binding heme groups. Structurally, the protein contains helix, transit peptide, and transmembrane domains, with 9 alpha helices, 5 beta strands, and 3 turns. It spans the inner mitochondrial membrane once, with the majority of the protein localized on the intermembrane side. The protein has covalent heme-binding sites at amino acid positions 121 and 124, as well as iron-metal binding sites at positions 125 and 244, which serve as axial ligands for the heme group. Functionally, the CYC1 protein is an integral part of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. It is a subunit of the cytochrome bc1 complex (complex III) and plays a pivotal role in electron transfer. Specifically, it facilitates the transfer of electrons from the Rieske iron-sulfur protein to cytochrome c, a critical step in cellular respiration. The CYC1 gene is highly conserved across a wide range of species, including chimpanzees, Rhesus monkeys, dogs, cows, mice, rats, zebrafish, fruit flies, mosquitoes, C. elegans, S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, E. gossypii, S. pombe, N. crassa, A. thaliana, rice, and frogs. Orthologs of the CYC1 gene have been identified in 137 different organisms, underscoring its evolutionary importance. Clinically, mutations in the CYC1 gene are associated with mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear, type 6. This is an autosomal recessive disorder of the mitochondrial respiratory chain caused by defects in Ubiquinol Cytochrome c Reductase (complex III), leading to reduced enzymatic activity. Symptoms of this condition typically manifest in early childhood and may include episodic acute lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, insulin-responsive hyperglycemia, liver dysfunction, encephalopathy, and susceptibility to infections. Despite these symptoms, psychomotor development may remain unaffected in some cases. Pathogenic mutations identified in this gene include c.288G>T (p.Trp96Cys) and c.643C>T (p.Leu215Phe). CYC1 is known to participate in 78 protein-protein interactions, with 72 of these being co-complex interactions. It is one of 11 subunits of the Ubiquinol Cytochrome c Reductase complex (cytochrome b-c1 complex), which also includes respiratory subunits such as cytochrome b, UQCRFS1, and other core proteins like UQCRC1 and UQCRC2. Additionally, the complex contains low-molecular-weight proteins such as UQCRH, UQCRB, UQCRQ, UQCR10, and UQCR11, as well as a cleavage product of UQCRFS1. Other proteins, including CCP1, CDKA-1, and CDKB1-1, have also been identified as interacting partners of CYC1.
